canonical_question: How can 'grain refinement' occur during dual-beam irradiation if the sample is simultaneously being heated or if defect recombination usually leads to growth?

question_variants.question: How can 'grain refinement' occur during dual-beam irradiation if the sample is simultaneously being heated or if defect recombination usually leads to growth?
question_variants.resolution_summary: Grain refinement during dual-beam irradiation (dropping to 21.1 nm) is attributed to a cascade effect from overlapping cascades larger than the grain size, which creates stacking faults and fragmentation, counteracting typical thermal growth.

answers.answer: Grain refinement occurred during dual-beam irradiation, dropping the average grain size to 21.1 ± 1.4 nm. This is attributed to a cascade effect where overlapping cascades larger than the grain size create stacking faults and fragmentation.
answers.mechanism: Cascade effect causing fragmentation and stacking faults.
evidence_spans: The results here demonstrate that grain refinement only occurred when the heavy ions are introduced.
This suggests that such a grain refinement observed in the dual-beam irradiation case was caused by a cascade effect.
The in situ nature of the experiments performed in this work has allowed us to observe the grain refinement effect in real-time

source_evidence_spans: However, during the dual-beam irradiation, grain refinement occurred, and the average grain size dropped to 21.1 ± 1.4 nm after a total irradiation time of ~94 mins.
